The datagoodr Workflow

workflow-overview.Rmd

This is the mental model, without the mechanics. One artifact — the DGF — is the spine of everything datagoodr does.

One artifact at the center

Most tools treat a data dictionary as a document you write about the data, off to the side. datagoodr treats it as the control center: a single table, one row per variable, that is at once a governed data dictionary and the thing that drives every downstream step.

                 ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  raw CSV  ─────▶│  DGF — one row per variable    │─────▶  governed CSV
                 │  • what it is  (type)          │        (stabilized)
   you curate ──▶│  • how to read it (rules)      │
                 │  • what it means (labels)      │─────▶  Research Guide
                 │  • how it looks  (profile)     │        (rendered profiles)
                 └───────────────────────────────┘

Everything flows through it: the raw data is profiled into it, you curate it, and both the stabilized dataset and the rendered guide are produced from it. Once the DGF exists, the raw data is no longer needed to render documentation.

Managing data types is the hinge

The reason one artifact can drive so much is that nearly everything follows from a column’s type. Settle whether a column is a date, a category, a count, or an identifier, and three things fall out automatically:

  • the stabilization rule that turns its raw form into a clean one,
  • whether it can be imported to that type or must be protected as text, and
  • the data profile and the visual used to render it.

So the workflow is really: get the types right (datagoodr guesses, you confirm), and let the rest follow.

A glimpse of the DGF

A DGF is an ordinary table — here are a few columns for four variables, the kind of thing you would scan in a spreadsheet:

 var_name     guess_label                     desired_data_type   stabilizer
 ----------   -----------------------------   -----------------   ---------------------------------
 founded      calendar {{ date :: temporal }} temporal            {{ read_mdy_slash :: write_yyyymmdd }}
 county_fips  us_state {{ ... :: identifier }} identifier          (protected as text)
 grade        number {{ quantity }}           categorical         (set by you — a grade is not a number)
 revenue      usd {{ currency :: number }}    number              {{ read_usd :: write_numeric }}

The guess_* columns are the machine’s first pass; the desired_* columns are your confirmed answer; the stabilizer is the rule that bridges them. Other columns (not shown) hold the profile and the dictionary text.

A glimpse of the data profiles

From each column’s type and values, datagoodr computes a profile and renders it with a type-appropriate visual. Two examples:

  • A numeric column (revenue) renders as a histogram with a quantile table — minimum, Q05/Q25/median/Q75/Q95, maximum, plus mean, skew, and kurtosis — and the universal quality counts (missing, zeros, distinct).
  • A categorical column (region) renders as a treemap with a frequency table, each level sized by its share, and the same universal quality counts.

A date would render as a calendar heat-map, a boolean as a two-bar chart, free text as a word cloud. The profile is chosen by type — which is why getting the types right is the whole game. (Data Profiling and Profiles & Research Guides go into each of these.)

The loop

Governance is not one-shot. You clean a column, correct a type, add a label; and update_dgf() reconciles the DGF with the new data — recomputing the profile for what changed while preserving everything you curated. The DGF is a living document, not a snapshot.
